name: Big A (打大A)
description: Big A (打大A, dǎ dà A) is a Chinese climbing game for exactly 5 players with variable partnerships, played with two standard 54-card decks (108 cards total including 4 Jokers). Before play, one player exposes an Ace to become the 'declarer' — the holder of the identical Ace (same rank and suit from the other deck) becomes their secret partner. Nobody knows who the partner is until they choose to reveal themselves. If the declarer holds both copies, they play alone against four opponents. Teams score based on the order in which their members empty their hands.

overview.description: Big A (打大A, dǎ dà A) is a Chinese climbing game for exactly 5 players with variable partnerships, played with two standard 54-card decks (108 cards total including 4 Jokers). Before play, one player exposes an Ace to become the 'declarer' — the holder of the identical Ace (same rank and suit from the other deck) becomes their secret partner. Nobody knows who the partner is until they choose to reveal themselves. If the declarer holds both copies, they play alone against four opponents. Teams score based on the order in which their members empty their hands.

history.origins: Big A originated in Inner Mongolia, China. It belongs to the large family of Chinese climbing games (shēng jí / 升级 family) that includes Dou Di Zhu and Tractor. The game's distinctive feature is the secret partnership mechanic based on matching identical Aces across two decks.
timeline: Late 20th century: Emerges in Inner Mongolia as a local climbing game.
2000s-2010s: Spreads across China via mobile apps and online platforms.
Present: Popular as a casual multiplayer game, especially in northern China.
history.cultural: Part of the rich tradition of Chinese climbing games. The social deduction aspect — figuring out who holds the matching Ace — adds an exciting layer of table talk and inference that makes the game popular in social settings.
history.evolution: Big A combines the climbing/shedding mechanics common to Chinese card games with a hidden-team mechanic reminiscent of games like Bǎo Huáng (保皇). The secret partner system creates a social deduction element layered on top of the climbing gameplay.

setup.deck: Two standard 54-card decks (2 × 52 + 4 Jokers = 108 cards). Each deck has a red Joker and a black Joker. Suits are irrelevant except for identifying matching Aces.
setup.dealing: Cards are drawn one at a time (as in other Chinese games). Players look at cards as they draw, except for the very last card drawn, which is kept face down temporarily. First three players get 22 cards; last two get 21. Play direction is anti-clockwise.

rules.objective: Empty your hand before opponents. The team of the player who goes out first wins; the team of the player who goes out last loses. Score depends on how quickly both team members empty their hands.
rules.gameplay: Cards are drawn one at a time anticlockwise; first three players get 22 cards each, last two get 21. During or after drawing, a player may expose an Ace to make it the Big Ace and become declarer; the holder of the matching Ace is the secret partner. Play: declarer or partner (if revealed) leads any single or combination. In turn each player passes or plays a higher combination of the same type. Four consecutive passes clear the pile and the last player leads again. First team to empty both hands wins; scoring is by finish order and doubles if partner revealed their Ace.
keyRules: Exposing the matching Ace reveals the partnership but doubles the score.
Four consecutive passes end a round — last player to play leads next.
Bombs beat any non-bomb combination and can be played at any time.
If declarer holds both Aces, they play alone (1 vs 4). They may surrender for a small penalty instead.
Suits don't matter for combinations — only for identifying matching Aces.

strategy.basic: As declarer, lead with your strong combinations to shed cards quickly. As the secret partner, help the declarer without revealing yourself too early — play high cards to support their leads.
strategy.intermediate: Partner revelation timing: revealing early doubles the score but makes you a target. Reveal late only if winning is certain. As an opponent, watch for suspicious play that suggests someone is helping the declarer.
strategy.advanced: Bomb management: holding a bomb gives you enormous power to interrupt opponents' leads. Save bombs for critical moments when opponents are about to go out. Social deduction: track which players pass on beatable combinations — they may be secretly helping the declarer.
tips: Don't expose both Aces immediately unless you have an extremely strong hand for solo play.
As the secret partner, subtle cooperation (not trumping the declarer's leads, helping clear their suits) is more valuable than flashy reveals.
Bomb timing is everything: playing a bomb too early wastes your best interruption tool.
Pay attention to card counts: know who has few cards left and prioritize stopping them.

variations.emptyOverridesReason: Bǎo Huáng is only referenced as a related game; full rule differences and engine overrides have not been modelled yet.

scoring.description: Zero-sum scoring. Points based on the order teammates finish. If partner's Ace was revealed before play, scoring is doubled. Solo declarer wins by finishing first, loses by finishing last.

synthesis.shortDescription: A 5-player Chinese climbing game from Inner Mongolia. Two decks, 108 cards, and a hidden partnership mechanic: the declarer exposes an Ace, and the holder of the matching Ace from the other deck is their secret ally. Social deduction meets card shedding. Bombs trump everything.
